# rebase --onto: cut a commit chain off one base and replay on another

After this page you can read `git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch>` as "take commits reachable from `<branch>` but not from `<upstream>`, and replay them onto `<newbase>`", run the classic "feature was based on topic; put it on main instead" transplant, and recover a topic after an upstream hard rebase.

## Thesis

Plain `git rebase main` replays *everything* after the merge-base with `main`. That is wrong when your branch contains commits you do **not** want to keep in the replay — for example a feature that started on `topic`, while `topic` itself should stay behind. **`--onto`** lets you name the new base and the cut point separately.

Verified with **git 2.47.3**.

## The form

```bash
git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>]
```

| Argument | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `<newbase>` | Where the rewritten commits should hang |
| `<upstream>` | Exclusive lower bound: commits reachable from here are *not* replayed |
| `<branch>` | Tip to rewrite (defaults to `HEAD`); checked out as part of the rebase |

In set language: replay `upstream..branch` onto `newbase`.

## Classic transplant

You built `feature` on top of `topic`. `topic`'s patches landed on `main` (or you no longer want `feature` to carry `topic`'s commits). You want only `feature`'s own commits on `main`:

```text
 before                         after
 main ──●──●                    main ──●──●── f1' ── f2'   (feature)
          \                              \
 topic ──── t1 ── t2                      t1 ── t2   (topic unchanged)
                \
 feature ──────── f1 ── f2
```

```bash
git rebase --onto main topic feature
```

## Lab

<!-- file: onto-lab.sh -->
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/onto-demo && mkdir /tmp/onto-demo && cd /tmp/onto-demo
git init -b main
git config user.name t
git config user.email t@t

echo base > a.txt && git add a.txt && git commit -m 'base'
git checkout -b topic
echo t1 > t.txt && git add t.txt && git commit -m 't1'
echo t2 >> t.txt && git commit -am 't2'
git checkout main
echo m1 >> a.txt && git commit -am 'main-moves'
git checkout -b feature topic
echo f1 > f.txt && git add f.txt && git commit -m 'f1'
echo f2 >> f.txt && git commit -am 'f2'

git rebase --onto main topic feature
git log --oneline --decorate --graph --all
```

Verified result on the authoring box:

```text
* dd5311f (HEAD -> feature) f2
* 4f67dab f1
* 85868ef (main) main-moves
| * 1854277 (topic) t2
| * cbf0871 t1
|/
* bd6ba60 base
```

`feature` now sits on `main`. `topic` is untouched. Commit hashes of `f1`/`f2` changed because rebase rewrites.

## Dropping a range

The same tool removes commits from the middle of a branch. Given `E--F--G--H--I--J` on `topicA`, this drops `F` and `G`:

```bash
git rebase --onto topicA~5 topicA~3 topicA
```

`--onto` and the upstream can be any commit-ish, not only branch names.

## Hard-case recovery after an upstream rewrite

If someone rebased `subsystem` that you based `topic` on, a plain `git rebase subsystem` only works when the patch-ids still match (easy case). When the upstream rebase edited, squashed, or conflict-resolved commits, you must name the *old* tip explicitly:

```bash
# old tip still in the reflog after fetch
git rebase --onto subsystem subsystem@{1}
```

or, if you know `topic` has three exclusive commits, `topic~3` as the old upstream tip. This is the "hard case" in the rebase man page — and everyone downstream of you may need the same transplant.

## Pitfalls

1. **Swapping arguments.** `--onto newbase upstream` — newbase first. Saying `--onto topic main feature` when you meant the reverse puts commits in the wrong place.
2. **Forgetting `<branch>` while on the wrong HEAD.** Always pass the branch name, or `checkout` first.
3. **Force-pushing a shared tip without coordination.** `--onto` rewrites hashes. Use a force-with-lease and tell collaborators.
4. **Expecting merge commits to survive.** Default rebase drops merges; use `--rebase-merges` only when you intend to rebuild topology.
5. **Skipping the log check.** After `--onto`, `git log --oneline --graph --all` should show the transplanted tip on the new base and the cut branch still where you left it.


## Compared with cherry-pick

`git cherry-pick A..B` can move a range onto `HEAD`, but you manage the checkout and the range endpoints yourself. `rebase --onto` packages "cut exclusive range + move branch tip" into one operation and updates the branch ref when it finishes. Prefer `--onto` when the tip you are rewriting should move; prefer cherry-pick when you want to copy commits onto another line without moving the source branch.

## Checklist before you force-push

1. `git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all` shows the transplanted tip on the intended base.
2. `git range-diff oldtip...newtip` (when available) summarises what changed in the rewrite.
3. Collaborators know the tip moves; open PRs retarget if needed.
4. Push with `git push --force-with-lease`.


## Summary

- `rebase --onto newbase upstream branch` replays `upstream..branch` onto `newbase`.
- Use it to detach a feature from an intermediate topic, or to drop a bad range.
- Hard-case recovery after an upstream rewrite is the same command with a reflog or relative old tip.
- Confirm with a graph log; then push with care.
